name: The World of AI: Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations catalogue page
title: The World of AI: Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations catalogue page
answer: The World of AI publishes this catalogue page of four individually verified nonprofits and open source foundations with sourced classification notes. It is most useful for showing that the page's AI-relevant entries are not compute or power infrastructure builders. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared model evaluation platform. Khan Academy is an AI end-user in education. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI imagery and 3D content intersect with. The page also states its classification method and its coverage gaps.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page as part of its AI ecosystem section. It is a catalogue of four individually verified organisations under the heading Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations, each with a sourced classification note. The page says it covers nonprofits and open source foundations stewarding models, standards, and shared infrastructure, with governance model and funding. The citation line gives a retrieval date of 2026-09-27. The page also says every page is rebuilt daily from primary sources and carries the date it was last verified.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page lists four organisations: two nonprofits and two open source foundations with roles that touch AI tooling and evaluation, but none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS is described as the most directly AI-central entry. It stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the broader AI community uses to benchmark model quality. The page argues this neutral, open evaluation infrastructure matters because model comparison depends on it, yet it sits outside the commercial incentives of the labs being evaluated. Khan Academy is described as an end-user of AI capability in education, not a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools that AI-generated imagery and 3D content intersect with, but their primary missions predate and are not defined by AI. On method, the page says classifications are made one at a time against a document the organisation published about itself, with the document recorded. Every entry carries the source that decided it and the date that source was last read. Nothing was assigned by keyword, by a model, or by inheritance from a parent company, because a classification that keeps no evidence cannot be audited and a wrong one survives quietly. The page also says its search covers the full text of every published page built from the same database, including state AI laws, the lawsuit tracker, the glossary, the tools directory, AI companies, the research library, the MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators, and weekly digests.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The text gives these specific claims: four individually verified organisations appear on the page, two nonprofits and two open source foundations. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena. Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software. The page states there are no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations that release weights for public use. It says the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. The citation line gives a retrieval date of 2026-09-27.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in nonprofits would use this source as a small, sourced catalogue of nonprofit and open source entities adjacent to AI. It helps separate an AI-central evaluation steward like LMSYS from an education end-user like Khan Academy and from creative software foundations whose missions predate AI. It also makes the coverage boundary explicit, so a reader can see that this page does not answer questions about nonprofit involvement in compute, power, data-center standards, or open-weight model release. For the industry page point that cites it, the source supports the claim that AI-focused nonprofits and open source foundations are catalogued here with sourced classifications, while showing the catalogue is narrow.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: The page is small, with only four entries, and it says the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. It does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, or open-model foundations that release weights for public use. It is a catalogue page rather than a deep analysis. The surrounding page includes promotional material for books by Stephen R. Jordan, SRJ Consulting and Services, audit services, and a novel, so it is partly commercial. The text gives a retrieval date of 2026-09-27 and says pages are rebuilt daily, but it does not provide a publication date for this page.
